summary.text: For \(n\ge100\), let \(d=D(n)\), \(e=D(d)\), and \(T=(n-e)/9\); digit-sum congruences modulo \(9\) make \(T\) integral, and padding the digits of \(d-1\) to length \(T\) and adjoining their digitwise \(9\)-complements produces a number \(k\) with \(D(k)=9T+e=n\) and \(d\mid k\), since the complementary block has value \(d(10^T-1)\). Thus \(k\ne n\) and the two divisibilities hold, while the remaining cases \(1\le n<100\) are settled by explicit partners.

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(m)\) denote the sum of the ordinary decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(m\). A positive integer \(k\ne n\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\) precisely when
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
We prove that every positive \(n\) has such a partner. This immediately proves the assertion about \(a(n)\): the set from which \(a(n)\) is chosen is then nonempty, and all its elements are positive, so its least element cannot be zero.

We first record some elementary facts about decimal digit sums.

If \(m>0\), write \(m=10q+r\), where \(0\le r<10\). Removing the final decimal digit gives
\[
D(m)=r+D(q). \tag{1}
\]
Also \(D(m)>0\) for \(m>0\), because the decimal representation of a positive number has at least one nonzero digit. The standard estimate
\[
D(m)\le m \tag{2}
\]
follows at once by induction from (1). In fact, if \(m\ge10\), then \(q\ge1\), and (1) and (2) give
\[
D(m)=r+D(q)\le r+q<r+10q=m. \tag{3}
\]
Every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its decimal digit sum. Consequently, for \(m\ge10\), the positive difference \(m-D(m)\) in (3) is divisible by \(9\). Thus
\[
D(m)+9\le m \qquad(m\ge10). \tag{4}
\]

A slightly stronger estimate will be needed. We claim that
\[
10D(m)\le m\qquad(m\ge100). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, again put \(m=10q+r\), with \(0\le r\le9\). Now \(q\ge10\), so (4) gives \(D(q)+9\le q\). Therefore
\[
10D(m)=10r+10D(q)
 \le 10D(q)+90
 \le 10q
 \le 10q+r=m.
\]
(The first inequality uses \(r\le9\).)

We next give a construction that works uniformly for every \(n\ge100\).

Fix such an \(n\), and set
\[
d=D(n),\qquad \delta=D(d).
\]
Since \(n>0\), we have \(d>0\). By (2), \(\delta\le d\), while (5) gives \(10d\le n\). Moreover,
\[
n\equiv d\equiv\delta\pmod 9.
\]
It follows that \(n-\delta\) is a nonnegative multiple of \(9\). Define
\[
T=\frac{n-\delta}{9}.
\]
Thus
\[
\delta+9T=n. \tag{6}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
9d+\delta\le9d+d=10d\le n,
\]
so (6) implies
\[
d\le T. \tag{7}
\]

We now describe a decimal digit list. Throughout this construction, digit lists are written from least significant digit to most significant digit. For such a list \(A=(a_0,\ldots,a_{s-1})\), put
\[
V(A)=\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}a_i10^i.
\]
If \(A\Vert B\) denotes concatenation, then
\[
V(A\Vert B)=V(A)+10^{|A|}V(B). \tag{8}
\]

Take the decimal digits of \(d-1\), and append enough zero digits at their most-significant end to obtain a list \(P\) of exactly \(T\) digits. This is possible because \(d-1<10^T\). To see this, (7) gives \(d-1<T\), and \(T<10^T\) for positive \(T\). Padding with zeros does not change the represented integer, so
\[
|P|=T,\qquad V(P)=d-1. \tag{9}
\]

Let \(C\) be the digitwise nine's complement of \(P\): every digit \(x\) of \(P\) is replaced by \(9-x\). Then \(|C|=T\). Two elementary complement identities are
\[
V(C)+V(P)=10^T-1, \tag{10}
\]
and
\[
\sum C+\sum P=9T. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, (11) follows because each corresponding pair of digits sums to \(9\), and (10) follows from
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{T-1}(9-p_i)10^i+
\sum_{i=0}^{T-1}p_i10^i
=9\sum_{i=0}^{T-1}10^i=10^T-1.
\]

Let
\[
B=C\Vert P.
\]
By (8), (9), and (10),
\[
\begin{aligned}
V(B)
 &=V(C)+10^T V(P)\\
 &=\bigl(10^T-1-(d-1)\bigr)+10^T(d-1)\\
 &=10^Td-d\\
 &=d(10^T-1).
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\]
Thus \(d\mid V(B)\). Notice also from (11) that the sum of all digits in \(B\) is \(9T\).

Finally, let \(Q\) be the list consisting first of one zero digit and then the ordinary digit list of \(d\), and define
\[
L=B\Vert Q,
\qquad k=V(L).
\]
The initial zero in \(Q\) shifts the digits of \(d\) one decimal place, so
\[
V(Q)=10d.
\]
Consequently \(d\mid V(Q)\). Equation (8), together with (12), now shows
\[
k=V(B)+10^{|B|}V(Q),

giving
\[
d\mid k. \tag{13}
\]

All entries in \(L\) are decimal digits. Its most significant digit is the most significant digit of the positive integer \(d\), hence is nonzero. Therefore \(L\) is exactly the ordinary decimal digit list of \(k\), including any internal zeros. Its digit sum is, by (6) and (11),
\[
D(k)=\sum L
     =\sum C+\sum P+0+D(d)
     =9T+\delta
     =n. \tag{14}
\]
In particular, \(k>0\), and (14) gives
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{15}
\]
Together, (13) and (15) are the two required divisibilities, since \(d=D(n)\).

It remains only to check that this constructed \(k\) is distinct from \(n\). If \(k=n\), then (14) would give
\[
D(n)=D(k)=n,
\]
so \(d=n\). But (5) would then say \(10n=10d\le n\), impossible because \(n>0\). Hence \(k\ne n\). We have therefore constructed a Harshad amicable partner for every \(n\ge100\).

It remains to handle \(1\le n\le99\). The following table supplies an explicit partner \(k\) for each such \(n\). In the table, \(d=D(n)\) and \(e=D(k)\). \[
\boxed{a(n)\ne0\quad\text{for every positive integer }n.}
\]
